client: Lately, I’ve been feeling so empty and unmotivated. I used to love painting and going for walks, but since losing my partner three months ago, it’s like I can’t even bring myself to pick up a brush or step outside. I guess I’m not sure if therapy can really help me feel like myself again—it just feels like nothing will ever be the same.
therapist: It sounds like this loss has left you feeling disconnected from the things that once brought you joy, and I can hear the genuine pain in your voice. Therapy can be a space to gently explore those feelings and gradually reconnect with what matters to you—would it feel helpful to talk more about what “feeling like yourself again” might look like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I don't even know what "feeling like myself" would look like anymore. That version of me who loved painting and exploring new hiking trails feels like a different person—someone I can't reach anymore. It's frustrating because part of me wants to try, but another part keeps saying "what's the point?" when I know they won't be there to share it with me.
therapist: It seems like there’s a real tension between wanting to reconnect with those parts of yourself and feeling held back by the pain of their absence. The frustration in your voice suggests this is really weighing on you—what do you think it would take to give yourself permission to explore those activities again, even in small ways?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I guess I’m scared that if I try to paint or go for a walk, it’ll just make me feel worse—like I’m pretending everything’s okay when it’s not. And honestly, I don’t even know where to start. The idea of picking up a brush or stepping outside feels overwhelming, like I’m staring at a mountain I can’t climb.
therapist: The way you describe this makes so much sense—it’s not about pretending things are okay, but about honoring where you are right now while taking tiny steps forward. What if we thought about this mountain as something you could approach one small foothold at a time, rather than needing to climb it all at once?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I see what you’re saying, but even small steps feel impossible right now. Like, I tried opening my sketchbook last week, but I just stared at the blank page and felt this wave of sadness. It’s like everything reminds me of them, and I don’t know how to separate those memories from the things I used to love. Maybe I’m just not ready yet.
therapist: It sounds like opening that sketchbook brought up a lot of emotions, and I can hear in your voice that it was a difficult moment. Maybe it’s not about being “ready” but about finding ways to approach these activities that feel manageable, even if they bring up sadness—what do you think that could look like for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess I could try something simpler, like just doodling or scribbling instead of trying to create a full painting. But even that feels scary because I keep thinking about how they used to sit next to me and watch me paint. It’s hard to imagine doing anything creative without feeling their absence so deeply.
therapist: It’s clear how much their presence meant to you, and I can hear the tenderness in your voice as you talk about those moments. Starting with something simple like doodling might be a way to honor both your creativity and your grief—does that feel like something you could gently explore, even if it’s just for a few moments?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Maybe I could try just a few minutes of doodling, but I worry it'll turn into me crying over the page. Part of me wants to avoid it completely because it hurts, but another part misses making art so much. It's like being stuck between two painful choices.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a real struggle between the part of you that misses creating and the part that’s afraid of the pain it might bring up. Could it be possible to let yourself cry if that happens, while still allowing space to reconnect with something you love? Sometimes, embracing both the sadness and the joy can be part of the healing process.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I haven’t really thought about it that way—letting myself cry while still trying to create. It’s just that when I’ve cried before, it feels like it’ll never stop, and I’m scared I won’t be able to pull myself back together. But maybe you’re right—maybe I don’t have to avoid it completely. It’s just hard to imagine finding any joy in it right now.
therapist: I can hear how overwhelming those moments of grief feel when they come up—it makes sense to worry about being pulled under by them. But there’s also a thoughtful openness in your voice as you consider this different approach, like you’re allowing yourself to explore what might be possible. What would it feel like to have some compassion for yourself if tears do come, rather than seeing it as something you need to "pull yourself together" from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I don't know if I can be compassionate with myself when I cry - it just feels like weakness. My partner was always the one who comforted me when I got upset, and now when I cry, it just reminds me they're not here to do that anymore. Maybe that's why I've been trying so hard to avoid letting myself feel anything.
therapist: It sounds like your tears feel especially lonely now without your partner’s comfort, and I can hear how much you’ve come to associate their support with being able to handle difficult emotions. That belief about weakness—where do you think that comes from? Sometimes our harshest judgments about ourselves are thoughts we’ve absorbed over time rather than truths.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: I never really thought about where that belief comes from... I guess growing up, my dad always said "big boys don't cry" whenever I got upset. But now that you mention it, my partner was the first person who ever made me feel safe being emotional. Without them, it's like I've gone back to that old way of thinking. It's just so hard to comfort myself when I've never really learned how.
therapist: It sounds like your partner helped you break away from that old mindset, and now that they’re gone, it’s understandable that those early messages about emotions might feel louder again. What do you think it would be like to challenge that idea that crying is a weakness, especially when it’s tied to something as meaningful as your loss?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I’ve never really questioned that belief—it’s just always been there, like a reflex. But now that you point it out, it does feel unfair to judge myself so harshly for grieving. It’s just hard to imagine how to comfort myself when I’ve always relied on others for that. Maybe I could try, but it feels like I’m starting from zero.
therapist: It sounds like you’re beginning to recognize that belief for what it is—a reflex, not a truth—and that’s a really important step. Starting from zero can feel daunting, but it’s also an opportunity to build a new relationship with your emotions, one where you can offer yourself the same compassion your partner once showed you. What might a small act of self-compassion look like for you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
